home.hero_photo_alt: The paved Larkspur bike path leading toward Mt. Tamalpais on a clear day
home.hero_intro: We’re a volunteer group of parents, riders and neighbors in Larkspur and Corte Madera. We work to give kids great places to learn and ride, safe ways to get around town, and a riding community that welcomes every family.
home.hero_h1b: Passing it on to the next generation
home.hero_bg_alt: Illustration of young mountain bikers on a ridge trail above Southern Marin at sunset, looking out over Richardson Bay and San Francisco
home.fact1_text: Larkspur kids — the Larkspur Canyon Gang — helped invent mountain biking on Mt. Tam. [SOURCE TO ADD]
home.fact2_text: Our kids share schools, streets and trails across Larkspur and Corte Madera.
home.fact3_text: No one is paid. We're neighbors doing this for the kids in our towns.
home.what_title: A voice for everyone on two wheels
home.what_intro: We live at the foot of one of the most famous riding landscapes in the world. We want every kid and family in Larkspur and Corte Madera to be able to enjoy it safely, close to home.
home.what_image_alt: Young riders standing in a line on a ridge trail with Mt. Tamalpais behind them
home.what1_icon_alt: Youth riding icon: a kid riding a pump track roller
home.what1_text: More kids want to ride than our towns have room for. A local middle school team had to turn riders away last year. We support skills parks, beginner-friendly trails and programs where young riders can learn before they take on Mt. Tam.
home.what2_icon_alt: Safe streets icon: a bicycle in a bike lane by a crosswalk
home.what2_text: Kids should be able to bike to school, practice and friends' houses safely. We back safe routes to school, connected paths and crossings, and smart e-bike education for teens and parents.
home.what3_icon_alt: Trails icon: a trail winding toward Mt. Tamalpais
home.what3_text: Riding is better together. We support family rides, trail-care days and ways to make bikes affordable, and we teach young riders to respect the trails and open space we share.
home.what4_icon_alt: Advocacy icon: a ballot going into a ballot box
home.what4_text: Decisions about where our kids ride are made at City Hall. We show up at council and commission meetings, and we endorse candidates who share our priorities.
home.about_intro: The Larkspur Corte Madera Bicycle Alliance is a volunteer community effort.
home.about_image_alt: A group of young mountain bikers on a dirt trail, cheering with their arms raised
home.join_intro: The more neighbors who show up, the more our towns listen. Here's how to help:

bike-park.hero_intro: We're working with the City of Larkspur to build a public pump track and progressive jump lines on the old dog park behind Hall Middle School — a safe, free place for local kids and families to build skills close to home.

bike-park.need_title: From zero to Mt. Tam, with nothing in between
bike-park.need_intro: Larkspur sits at the foot of one of the most famous mountain biking landscapes in the world. But new riders have no safe, local place to learn balance, cornering and jumping before they face steep, technical mountain trails.
bike-park.need_image_alt: Young riders standing in a line on a ridge trail with Mt. Tamalpais behind them
bike-park.need1_text: Beginners currently learn on Mt. Tam itself. A pump track and progressive jump lines let kids build skills in a controlled space first.
bike-park.need2_text: Youth riding in Larkspur is growing fast. Teams are turning kids away, and there's no local facility to absorb them.
bike-park.need3_text: Larkspur riders go on to the Redwood and Archie Williams high school mountain bike teams. [RANKINGS + SOURCE TO ADD]
bike-park.need4_text: A public facility for all ages and abilities — no club fees, no lift tickets, just a bike and a helmet.

endorsements.endorse_intro: The City Council shapes where our kids can ride, how safe our streets are, and how we care for our open space. These candidates understand why that matters to Larkspur families.
endorsements.endorse_question1: What are your thoughts on establishing one or more bike parks in Larkspur? What benefits or concerns do you see for our community?
endorsements.endorse_question2: If elected, what specific actions would you be willing to take to help make a bike park a reality? For example, how would you approach identifying suitable locations, working with the community, and securing funding?
endorsements.endorse_banner_alt: Candidates endorsed by the Larkspur Corte Madera Bicycle Alliance
endorsements.cand1_blurb: Walter strongly supports a Larkspur bike park as a safe, legal place for young riders to build skills and gather, while addressing location, neighborhood, environmental, liability, and maintenance concerns early. He proposes reviewing city and school district sites, involving riders and neighbors in design, pursuing public-private funding, establishing a maintenance plan, and publishing a clear project timeline.
endorsements.cand1_response1:
I'm strongly in favor. Marin is the birthplace of mountain biking, and Redwood High has one of the best mountain bike teams in the country. Yet our kids have very few legal, safe places close to home to build their skills. Most of our open space and parks are still off-limits to bikes. As a result, Marin has lost much of its riding heritage to places that welcomed it, while towns like Fairfax have taken a clearly pro-bike stance. Larkspur should be one of them.

The benefits go well beyond riding. A bike park gives kids and teens a healthy, screen-free place to gather, take smart risks, and learn from each other. It eases pressure on illegal trail use. And it brings families into the heart of town. Stafford Lake Bike Park shows what's possible when a community partners with Larkspur Recreation: it's well used, well loved, and a model for financial stewardship.

The concerns are real and solvable: site selection, neighbor impacts such as noise and parking, environmental review, liability, and long-term maintenance. They should be addressed openly and early, not used as reasons to stall.
endorsements.cand1_response2:
My whole campaign is about execution over talk, and this is a good test of it.

- Location: I'd ask staff for a quick inventory of city-owned and underused parcels. That includes the old dog park behind Hall Middle School. It comes with financial obligations and environmental constraints, but I'd want us to try everything we can to make it work. I'd also look at a joint-use agreement with the school district, since students are the core users.
- Community: I'd bring in the Parks & Rec Commission, Redwood's MTB team, families, MCBC, and neighbors from the start, with a design process young riders help shape.
- Funding: I'd follow the Stafford Lake model of a public-private partnership: grants, private and foundation donors, local businesses, and volunteer build days. That keeps the burden off the general fund, and a dedicated maintenance plan would be agreed before we break ground.
- Follow-through: I'd put a clear timeline on it and report progress publicly.
endorsements.cand2_blurb: Burnett supports a bike park as a way to help children ride safely, build confidence, and enjoy the outdoors while protecting the environment. He proposes championing the project through the Parks and Recreation Commission, maintaining community involvement, and pursuing partnerships and grants with county agencies, nonprofits, and state and federal programs.
endorsements.cand2_response1:
I was excited to learn about your efforts to establish a bike park in Larkspur. I bike to work every day, and my wife and I are raising a growing family here. I want my kids to grow up riding, and to learn in places built for it, not by dodging cars or weaving around people on a crowded path.

You can count on me to be a strong champion of projects that improve the welfare of our children, expand their access to the outdoors, and make biking and walking safer. A bike park has the potential to do all of that, giving young riders a safe place to build skills and confidence, get outside with friends, and become safer riders on the way to school, downtown, or the trails.

I also firmly believe Larkspur can improve its community assets while honoring our shared commitment to preserving the natural environment. Those goals aren't in conflict. With thoughtful planning and input from riders, parents, neighbors, and environmental stewards, projects like this can strengthen both.
endorsements.cand2_response2:
Good projects happen when local advocates and government work hand in hand. That's the work I do professionally, bringing community leaders and local government together to turn shared priorities into real results. In San Rafael, for example, I'm working with the City on a bicycle and pedestrian bridge that would connect the Canal neighborhood to the high school and downtown.

I'd bring that same approach to Larkspur. The Parks and Recreation Commission is the right place for proposals like this to be developed and vetted, and I'd respect that process. Respecting the process doesn't mean standing on the sidelines, though. As a Councilmember, I'd champion this effort by ensuring a lasting commitment to authentic community engagement, keeping riders, parents, neighbors, and local bicycle advocates at the table and partnering with them to find an option that works for Larkspur and respects the environment.

Funding would take some creativity, since the City's budget is limited. I'd look to partnerships with Marin County Parks and the Transportation Authority of Marin, along with state and federal grants that local nonprofits and county agencies could pursue together. With a community as committed as yours, a bike park is well worth pursuing. If elected, I would bring a strong commitment to helping build a Larkspur where every kid, including my own, can ride safely and enjoy the outdoors.
endorsements.cand3_blurb: Jaffe strongly supports a dedicated Larkspur bike park as a safe, sanctioned place for young riders and riders of all ages to build skills. He proposes evaluating sites beneath Highway 101 on the north side of Corte Madera Creek, at Hamilton Park, and near Hall Middle School, while championing private fundraising and bicycle-industry sponsorships.
endorsements.cand3_response1: I fully support creating a dedicated bike park in Larkspur. As one of the founding locations for mountain biking, and home to one of the most competitive youth mountain biking teams in the country, I can hardly think of a better place than Larkspur for a city-owned bike park. I also know that without such a facility, young riders hone their bike riding skills in unsanctioned locations, which is not a great solution for anyone. Encouraging youth (and riders of all ages) to get outside and improve their bike riding skills is a clear benefit to the community and something I would strongly support if elected to City Council.
endorsements.cand3_response2: I think the key is finding a suitable location. One idea I have had, and shared with Rob Webb, is below the 101 bridge on the north side of Corte Madera Creek. This site is currently underutilized and the substantial road noise makes it unsuitable for many uses. However, it may be an ideal location for a bike park. Hamilton Park and the north side of the Hall Middle School soccer field have also been mentioned as potential locations. I would support investigating all of these as the home for a future bike park. The funding for any future park is also a challenge, as there are clearly many competing budget priorities in a town of our size. But I would be very happy to champion a private fundraising campaign. I think with support from City Council, we could explore sponsorship opportunities from bicycle-related companies, leaning into our town's claim to be the "Birthplace of Mountain Biking".
